title: Stress and Strain in Emergency Physicians
summary:
Emergency physicians face significant physical and mental demands in their work. This is especially true for the staff of the specialized emergency medical vehicle at Heidelberg University Hospital (MIC), who are also deployed in the operating room and thus bear a double burden. Prolonged stress takes a toll on the body: It affects the nervous system, can lead to chronic physical strain, and impair performance during emergencies. To quantify this stress, various physiological indicators can be measured, such as heart rate variability, levels of the stress hormone cortisol in saliva, changes in electrocardiogram (ECG) patterns, and eye movements, which reveal insights into mental strain.
The goal of the planned study is to determine the extent to which emergency physicians experience stress while working at the MIC and in the operating room, and how well they recover from it. To this end, various measurement methods will be used simultaneously: eye movements, changes in the electrocardiogram, the stress hormone in saliva, a questionnaire for personal assessment of stress levels, and heart rate variability. In addition, the study will examine how individual, particularly stressful situations affect these metrics compared to repeated stress.
Forty emergency physicians from the MIC are participating in the study. Measurements are taken at three different times: at rest (as a baseline), during a normal workday at the hospital, and during a call with the MIC. The analysis focuses primarily on heart rate variability, eye movements, and changes in the electrocardiogram. In addition, pupil responses, eye movements, cortisol levels in saliva, and the participants’ personal assessment of stress are also evaluated.
The results are intended to help better understand how stress affects the decision-making ability of emergency physicians. In the long term, these findings will be used to develop measures to prevent the health consequences of stress, improve shift scheduling in emergency medical services, and enhance both patient care and workplace safety. The combination of multiple measurement methods is intended to ensure that the study’s objectives are reliably achieved.
conditions: Health consequences of stress, workload, patient safety, quality of care

interventions.name: Central to the research question is the data collection from 40 healthy emergency physicians who staff the MIC (Medical Intervention Car) at the Heidelberg Department of Anesthesiology.  The study does not include regular emergency physicians. The Medical Intervention Car (MIC) is a vehicle concept

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
•    MIC emergency physicians and/or RTH emergency physicians
•    Granting of written consent
•    Completion of one MIC or RTH assignment during the observation period
Exclusion criteria:
•    Known pregnancy
•    Pre-existing heart disease (valvular heart disease > Class I),
•    Any form of cardiomyopathy or channelopathy that can be diagnosed by ECG, echocardiogram, or exercise testing
•    History of coronary artery disease
•    History of myocarditis
•    Known high-frequency (> 1% of all beats within 24 hours) premature atrial or ventricular beats, atrial fibrillation, or conduction disturbances
•    Any antiarrhythmic therapy
•    Any implanted cardiac device
•    Known overt hyperthyroidism
